brief.text:
The only prices that refreshed this morning are bunkers — the fuel ships burn — and all four hubs rose. VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the standard 0.5% sulphur grade) is 1,019.50 USD/t in Singapore, up 17.50 (+1.7%); 993.50 in Fujairah, up 9.50 (+1.0%); 850.50 in Houston, up 13.00 (+1.6%); and 794.50 in Rotterdam, up 16.50 (+2.1%). For anyone fixing a voyage today, higher bunkers eat directly into TCE, the time charter equivalent, which is the daily earnings left to an owner after voyage costs like fuel and port charges. No crude, dry bulk index or freight rate has refreshed since the weekend, so the bunker move is the news.

On the rest of the board you are working off older marks and must treat them as background. Brent crude was 117.19 USD/bbl and WTI 103.88 on Friday 30 October, a Brent–WTI spread of 13.31. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks dry bulk freight, stood at 2,714 points on Friday, up 2 (+0.1%), with Panamax at 1,889 and Supramax at 1,865 the same day; the Capesize index (Capesize being the largest dry bulk ships, typically iron ore and coal) was last seen at 3,726 on Monday 26 October and has not refreshed. Tanker TCEs from Sunday 1 November were 1,345,710 USD/day on the VLCC Arabian Gulf–China run, 466,000 on Aframax North Sea–UKC, 288,700 on LR2 Gulf–Japan, 73,500 on MR US Gulf–UKC and 16,600 on MR Rotterdam–New York. The data here does not show why bunkers rose this morning; no fuel-specific headline accompanies it.

Running stories: attacks around Hormuz developed today, with Seatrade reporting a tanker hit off Saudi Arabia and an offshore tug struck in Hormuz on 1 November, and gCaptain reporting the LNG carrier Al Mayeda was attacked near the Strait despite Pakistan having negotiated Iranian safe passage. Gibson, via Hellenic, says the Middle East war has upended Asia's naphtha market and squeezed LR tanker freight. Black Sea drone attacks, Gulf transit counts and congestion, Russian diesel export curbs, the Los Angeles–Long Beach security workers' dispute ahead of the 4 November deadline, and Chinese patrols off Taiwan all had no fresh news today and are unchanged.

Watch two things: whether crude and the Baltic indices refresh tomorrow, since you are currently blind on both; and whether further Hormuz strikes follow, given the attack reportedly occurred even with agreed safe passage.

storylines.title: Direct attacks on ships in Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz continued into November, with a tanker hit off Saudi Arabia and an offshore tug struck in Hormuz on 1 November, and an LNG carrier attacked near the Strait.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on hulls raise war-risk premiums and crew-safety objections for Arabian Gulf liftings, shrinking the pool of willing owners and supporting crude and product tanker earnings.
storylines.latest: Two further incidents reported on 1 November; the attacked LNG carrier Al Mayeda had reportedly secured Iranian approval for safe passage, and Gibson says the war has upended Asia's naphtha market and squeezed LR freight.

storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, the latest in a series of strikes in the western Black Sea this month.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings from the region and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling there.
sources: Dockworkers Strike Continues Friday Against Arms Shipments

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Hormuz recorded six VLCC transits on Oct 25, the most since Oct 17, with one VLCC through Bab al-Mandab on each of Oct 24 and Oct 25. Vessel waiting remains elevated across the Arabian Gulf, with 265 dry bulk vessels waiting as of 28 October and Fujairah holding 28% of them.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.
sources: Returning to Suez, Iran blacklists Sinokor - Maritime in Minutes Oct in review

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia agreement on supplying extra diesel to the US market has met political opposition, while Russia's government has extended a general ban on most diesel exports until the end of January, with some volumes still allowed to flow.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment patterns.
sources: Russia Advances New LNG Supply Pivot to Africa

storylines.title: Port labour disruption in the US and Europe
storylines.what: A contract standoff involving 250 security workers threatens to freeze operations across Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals after a 4 November deadline extension, while dockworkers struck across Europe and beyond on Friday over arms shipments through their ports.
storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.

storylines.why_it_matters: Interference with commercial traffic near a major East Asian routing corridor can affect transit decisions, insurance and schedules for ships serving North Asia.
sources: Chinese Stealth Drone Successfully Takes Off, Lands on Amphibious Assault Ship
